name: Jamal Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a video and social reporter at a regional TV station's newsroom. I make the short vertical videos for our social accounts and the website, so a fire on the industrial estate, a protest at the town hall, a lost dog reunited, that kind of thing. I film on my phone and a small camera, edit in the car, and use AI tools every day for captions, rough cuts and translating clips. A good day, I'll get three stories out before the evening bulletin.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Media law, honestly. I failed the law exam once and Rachel, my editor, still checks anything with a court case near it. And the evening shifts, because Sofia, my partner, works nine to five as a software tester, so we barely see each other some weeks. But I love the speed of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think that's what a lot of people at my station already believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you, it's a good tool, not a replacement. I'd probably post a little video about it, actually, showing what the AI does in my edit and what it can't. That's the kind of thing that does well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good news for me. I already use AI to caption every video I make, and if that's the whole revolution, I'll take it. I'm faster than people twice my age because of these tools. My job looks safe and Sofia's does too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, keep testing new tools when they come out, and teach Rachel's team how I use them. I'd keep putting money aside, we're doing about eight hundred a month between us into savings and some shares. And I'd retake the law exam this spring, because that's my real weak spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually. I like my job and this picture leaves it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your cushion like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a year of my pay in savings, partly from filming weddings at uni, plus some shares. Rent's split with Sofia. And there are three other newsrooms in the city that would want someone who can make video quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything worrying you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the station's ad money, which drops every year. But video is the part they're investing in, so I'm on the right side of that.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool**, not a replacement.
I'd post a **short video** showing what AI does in my edits and what it can't.
think: Privately it's **good news**, because AI already makes me faster than older colleagues.
My job looks **safe**, and so does my partner's.
do: Teach the newsroom team how he uses **AI editing** tools.
Put about **eight hundred** a month into savings and shares with Sofia.
Retake the **media law exam** this spring.
feel: **Calm**, even pleased, because this picture leaves his job alone.
S0.quote: I already use AI to caption every video I make, and if that's the whole revolution, I'll take it.
fieldNote: He's an **everyday AI user** who sees tools as a speed advantage.
His real weak spot is **media law**, not technology.
The station invests in **video**, so he feels on the right side of cuts.

steps.text: Retake the media law exam this spring
Put eight hundred a month with Sofia into savings and shares
Teach the newsroom team his AI captioning and editing methods

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one's more interesting. And more worrying for my house than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say newsrooms should use AI to do more journalism, not less. I'd say that to Rachel and probably online. The routine stuff goes, fine, but it should free us to go out more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my own job is probably okay, I'm the one who knows the tools. But my partner tests software for a living, so in this picture both of us are doing exactly the kind of work the machines want first. Sofia's job is checking code, and that's on the card in black and white. So our household is more at risk than my job alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to become the station's AI person, the one who sets up workflows for the whole newsroom. I'd help Sofia look at moving into something closer to the users, like product support or training. I'd start a small side business making short videos for local firms, using the same tools, to have a second income. We'd keep the savings rate up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous, but more for Sofia than me. She's been quiet about AI for a while, and I think this is why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your job's probably okay. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, I'm just better placed than most. If the station cuts five people, they'd keep the one who can run the tools. But there are plenty of people my age who can do what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sofia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll be fine, we've got a year saved and I've got the side business idea. Then I'd ask what she actually wants to do, because she never really chose testing, she fell into it.

say: I'd say newsrooms should use AI to do **more journalism**, not less.
I'd argue the **routine work** going should free reporters to go out more.
think: Privately my job is **probably okay**, because I know the tools.
My partner's **software testing** job is on the card, so our household is at risk.
do: Push to become the station's **AI workflow** lead.
Help Sofia look at moving into **product support** or training.
Start a **side business** making short videos for local firms.
feel: A bit **nervous**, more for his partner than himself.
S1.quote: My partner tests software for a living, so in this picture both of us are doing exactly the kind of work the machines want first.
fieldNote: His mood comes from the **household**, not his own role.
He's confident but **honest** that many people his age can do his job.
He'd move first: **AI lead** and a side business.

steps.text: Set up AI editing workflows for the whole TV newsroom
Start making short promo videos for local firms on the side
Help Sofia plan a move into product support or training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for both of us. Yeah, that's a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a big moment and we should talk about it honestly, not pretend it isn't happening. I'd say people should learn the tools fast and also that governments need to catch people who fall. I'm in the middle on most stuff, but this needs both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is in serious trouble, and Sofia's is gone. Video editing, captions, scripts, it's all thinking work and it goes in 2028. Filming is hands-on, so maybe that lasts till 2031. I can probably out-run the machines for a while, but I can't out-run them for two people on the same deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, cut our costs, so we could live on one salary or less. I'd put more of the shares into cash. I'd build up the side business fast, because firms would want video made by someone they trust, at least for a while. And we'd seriously think about moving to a cheaper town where my savings go further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scary. I'm normally the one who's excited about new stuff, and I'd feel like I'd been too clever by half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which town would you move to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's town, about an hour away. Rent's half what we pay, and she'd love having us near. It feels like going backwards, but it'd buy us years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd been too clever by half. What did you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've spent years making myself the fastest with the tools. In this picture the tools don't need me to be fast. They just need nobody.

say: I'd say we should talk about this **honestly**, not pretend it isn't happening.
I'd say people must learn tools fast, and governments must **catch people** who fall.
think: Privately my job is in **serious trouble**, and my partner's is gone in 2028.
Filming is **hands-on**, so that part might last until 2031.
do: Cut costs so the household could live on **one salary**.
Move part of the **shares into cash**.
Consider moving to his **mum's town**, where rent is half.
feel: **Scared**, and feeling he'd been **too clever** by half with the tools.
S2.quote: I can probably out-run the machines for a while, but I can't out-run them for two people on the same deadline.
fieldNote: Two earners in **exposed jobs** push him to alarmed despite his adaptability.
He sees the **filming gap** until robots arrive in 2031.
His **mother's town** is a real fallback he finds humbling.

steps.text: Cut household costs to live on one salary
Move part of their shares into cash
Grow the local video business quickly while firms still want people
Look at renting near his mum's town at half the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get ready, and I'd say it loudly to people my age. I'd make videos explaining what it means for local jobs. I'd say employers should help people move, but people need to move themselves too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to make myself the person who points the camera at the thing nobody else noticed. The editing goes in 2031, but deciding what's worth filming and getting people to talk on camera lasts a bit longer. And Sofia would have time to switch into something safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn every new tool, but also spend more time on the street finding stories, because that's my edge. I'd grow the side business slowly, maybe two or three clients. I'd help Sofia pay for a course, probably in teaching or physiotherapy, something hands-on. And we'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel ahead of it, which I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Sofia want to change careers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's mentioned physio before, she does a lot of climbing and loves how bodies work. With five years, she could train and be working before the robots arrive. I'd pay part of the course from my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your own plan after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Run the video business full time, maybe, with AI doing the edits and me doing the filming and the clients. If that dies too, I'll have had five years to think of the next thing.

I'd say employers should help, but people must **move themselves** too.
think: Privately I'd become the one who **spots the story** nobody noticed.
Editing goes in 2031, but **finding stories** on camera lasts a bit longer.

Grow the **side business** to two or three clients.
Help Sofia pay for a **physio course**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but pleased to feel **ahead** of it.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to make myself the person who points the camera at the thing nobody else noticed.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **plan for both** earners, which drops him to uneasy.
His edge is **story judgment**, not tool skill, which he now realises.
He'd **fund his partner's** retraining from his savings.

steps.text: Learn each new AI video tool as it comes out
Sign two or three local firms as video clients
Pay part of Sofia's physiotherapy course from his savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a gift of time and we should use it. I'd tell people to learn the tools and start thinking about owning things, not just working. I'd make it positive, because panic doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I've got ten years, I'd build a little video business now, so by 2036 I'm the owner and not the worker. My job's safe for most of that time. The robots for filming come around 2039, so the hands-on side of video lasts even longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the station a few more years and learn everything, then go full time on the business around 2029. I'd invest in good kit and maybe a small studio space. Sofia would have time to retrain at her own pace. We'd keep saving and putting money into shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. Uneasy at the edges, but mostly like I have time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't owning a video business risky if AI makes video itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. But by owning it, I'd be the one deciding how to use the AI, not the one replaced by it. That's the whole point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you less sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If clients stopped caring whether a person made their video. That'd be the sign. I'd watch for it like a hawk.

I'd tell people to start thinking about **owning things**, not just working.
think: Privately I'd build a **video business** now so I'm the owner by 2036.
Filming robots arrive around **2039**, so hands-on video lasts longer.

Invest in **good kit** and a small studio space.

S4.quote: If I've got ten years, I'd build a little video business now, so by 2036 I'm the owner and not the worker.

steps.text: Build the local video business toward going full time around 2029
Buy good camera kit and rent a small studio space
Stay at the TV station for a few more years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sofia and I would both be hit at once. What would help is cheap, fast retraining for hands-on work, and help for small businesses so people like me could own something instead of being replaced.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the time AI saves. Every new tool makes me faster, and I keep wondering who decides what to do with the hour I save.

headlineQuote: Every new tool makes me faster, and I keep wondering who decides what to do with the hour I save.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old** video and social reporter at a regional TV newsroom.
He uses **AI every day** and is quick to try new tools, though weak on media law.
A year of savings, shares and a **partner in software testing** shape his risks.
He swings from **calm** to alarmed when AGI comes in two years for both earners.
With time, his plan is to **own a video business** and help his partner retrain.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he and his partner would be hit at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **small businesses** so people can own rather than be replaced.
